title.value: Ivarre on how the block groups take their turns at the pan

description.value: Interview cut into salt with the survey's steadiest informant on the pan, covering the rotation of block groups and what is traded for a turn. Recorded two years before contact was suspended.

content.value:
Cut over one working day. Each answer is a block; the survey's questions were cut shallow at the block edge in the same hand.

Q. May we lift the blocks and take them to the camp?

A. You are asking to carry a sentence out of the room. Cut what you want onto your own material. These stay until the flood.

Q. How is the order of turns settled?

A. By the block group holders, at the rim, before the water goes down. It takes an afternoon and it looks like nothing.

Q. Settled on what?

A. On who owes whom. A turn on the second channel mouth is worth four turns anywhere else and everyone knows it, so the second mouth is not taken, it is bought.

Q. Bought with what?

A. With debt carried from the last flood, which nobody can prove, because the last flood took the cutting that recorded it. That is not a flaw. That is why anyone agrees to any of it.

Q. Do the pan officers know?

A. They set it. They take a share of the second mouth in every rotation and have since before I was cutting. If you write that down in a language that stays, you should know what you are doing.

Q. We will write it down.

A. Then you will be sent off this world, and it will be about this, and the officers will give a different reason and it will be a good one.

consentNote.value: Ivarre consented to the survey's transcription and refused the removal of the blocks, on the ground that a statement here is unmade by flooding and a statement that cannot be unmade is a different kind of thing. He was explicit that he understood the transcription outlives the flood and cut the last block anyway.
